cues.text: An Ancient Church on the Maas

The church at Meerssen, in the southeastern Netherlands, traced its origins to a small chapel that had been enlarged in the mid-tenth century with the support of Gerberga of Saxony, wife of the French king Louis IV.
By the early thirteenth century it had grown into an important regional church, though nothing yet marked it as a future pilgrimage destination.
Blood at the Breaking of the Host
That changed, tradition holds, during a Sunday Mass in 1222.
As the priest broke the large consecrated host, living blood is said to have begun to drip from it, staining the corporal spread beneath.

Word of the sign spread through the region, and the church's ecclesiastical authorities at the time are said to have recognized it as a genuine Eucharistic wonder, drawing pilgrims to Meerssen from across the Low Countries.
The Miracle of the Fire
Meerssen's tradition did not end there.
In 1465, a devastating fire broke out and destroyed much of the church.

According to local memory, a farmer who saw the flames rushed inside and managed to rescue the blood-stained relic before the building was consumed, and found it completely unharmed by the fire that had destroyed everything around it.
The townspeople remembered this second sign as the "Miracle of the Fire," and the church was rebuilt around the same relic that had now survived both its founding wonder and near-destruction.
A Basilica and an Unbroken Procession
The rebuilt church continued to draw pilgrims across the following centuries.
In 1938, Pope Pius XI formally raised it to the rank of minor basilica, today known as the Basilica of the Blessed Sacrament.
It is dedicated jointly to the Holy Sacrament and to St. Bartholomew the Apostle.

The relic is still carried each year in procession through the town on the octave of Corpus Christi, a devotion that has continued, with interruptions only for the upheavals of history, for the better part of eight centuries.
Legacy

We find in Meerssen a tradition marked less by a single dramatic moment than by endurance — a sign given once during an ordinary Sunday Mass, and then, remarkably, preserved a second time through fire that consumed everything around it.
For a community that has now carried the same relic in procession for nearly eight hundred years, the deeper lesson may be less about wonder.
It may be less about any single event than about fidelity itself: a town's willingness, across war, reformation, and fire alike, to keep returning to the same small relic and unbroken thanksgiving.
